articles.title: When the Market Destroys a Community
articles.author: Evelina Johansson Wilén
articles.content_excerpt: In 1985, when I was four months old, my family moved from Kiruna to Luleå, a city in northern Sweden. My father had found a job with the Swedish State Railways, and we were given a firsthand rental contract for a four-room apartment in Hertsön, one of the city’s largest housing estates. Hertsön had been built as part of Sweden’s massive public housing program of the 1960s and ’70s. But there was another reason for its construction. It was meant to house workers for a vast new industrial project: Steelworks 80 (Stålverk 80). Steelworks 80 was conceived in the early 1970s by Sweden’s Social Democratic government as an expansion of the country’s steel industry. articles.title: 25 Years After 9/11, the Zombie War on Terror Stumbles On
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content_excerpt: What does it mean to “Never Forget,” as we’re often asked to do when it comes to the September 11 attacks that killed nearly three thousand people? After all, few people who witnessed the crime in real time could ever forget it or the horrors in its wake: the bodies falling, the survivors crushed beneath rubble and dust, the people riddled with disease years later.Certainly, “Never Forget” means keeping alive the memory of those whose lives were tragically lost. It could also be to remember and hold accountable those who perpetrated the crime. articles.title: Why Is It So Hard to Imagine the End of American Empire?
articles.author: Daniel Bessner
articles.content_excerpt: The September 11, 2001, attacks on New York City and Washington, DC, as the saying goes, “changed everything.” After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, the global American empire, created in the 1940s to combat communism, was left without a raison d’être . While foreign policymakers spent the 1990s searching for one, the best they could come up with — use the military power of the United States to stop humanitarian abuses abroad — was quixotic at best, catastrophic at worst. For a time, the empire lost its juice. The attacks changed all that. After 9/11, the United States identified a new global mission: fight “jihadist terrorism” wherever it might be found. After a few minutes, the first turns to the second and asks, “How can you read that garbage?” The second replies, “When I read your paper, it’s nothing but bad news. It depresses me! It cheers me up!” I kept thinking of that yesterday as I watched the first night of the Republicans’ midterm “ convention ” (where no one was nominated, and no official business of any kind was conducted). articles.title: Found, But Not Rescued
articles.content_excerpt: In the middle of the ocean, a man was drowning. He could not hold fast to the ropes dangling from the bow and stern of the bulk carrier that stopped to help. Below, a small, blue wooden boat crammed with people was tossed by a raging storm. As high winds sloshed water over the deck, the passengers — who had sailed for a day and a night without drinking water — rushed toward the swaying ropes. But the lines slipped through their hands. The children lacked the strength to climb. articles.title: Train Crashes Destroyed Their Towns. Will Yours Be Next?
articles.content_excerpt: Nearly 10 years before the train derailment and subsequent chemical disaster in East Palestine, Ohio, the town of Lac-Mégantic, Quebec experienced one of the deadliest rail disasters in North America. On July 6 , 2013 , a runaway train derailed in the center of town, leveling buildings and dumping millions of tons of crude oil onto the surrounding area. 47 people were killed in the explosion. In July , Maximillian Alvarez and Dr. Nicole Fabricant sat down with a panel of guests from East Palestine and Lac-Mégantic to discuss what happens when your town becomes a sacrifice zone and how residents can join together to fight back against the corporations responsible. articles.title: In the Name of Security
articles.content_excerpt: When Karla Padilla started her sentence at the federal correctional institution in Dublin, Calif., in 2023 , a guard singled her out. Over the next 15 months, the guard strip-searched Padilla so frequently that anyone near her risked being searched too, and other inmates began keeping their distance whenever that guard was on shift. Most prisons across the country conduct strip searches under a federal policy that requires women officers to inspect incarcerated women. The officer instructs them to remove their clothes, shake their hair, open their mouths, lift their breasts or genital area and then bend, squat and cough. articles.author: Nicholas Liu
articles.content_excerpt: Although the University of Chicago bears “Let knowledge grow from more to more; and so be human life enriched” as its official motto, a different slogan entirely has attained much wider fame. Thanks to long-cemented campus lore, the university is best known instead by the refrain of its student body: “Where fun goes to die.” The slogan is spoken in weary, ironic tones, suggesting a strange marriage of acceptance and self-congratulation.
